title: What to Eat After Throwing Up From Drinking: A Step-by-Step Plan
excerpt: Threw up after drinking? Start with slow sips of fluid, then broth, then bland foods like crackers, toast, and bananas. Here's the step-by-step plan, what to avoid, and when to get help.
metaDescription: What to eat and drink after throwing up from alcohol: a rehydrate-first plan, the best bland foods, what to avoid, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: what to eat after throwing up
content:
**The answer first:** after throwing up from drinking, don't eat yet. Rest your stomach for 15 to 30 minutes, then sip fluids, ideally an oral rehydration drink like Pedialyte or plain water. Once you've kept liquids down for an hour or two, move to clear broth, then bland starches like saltine crackers, dry toast, white rice, a banana, or applesauce. Add easy protein like scrambled eggs or plain chicken later in the day. Skip greasy food, coffee, fizzy drinks, and more alcohol until your stomach has settled.

That order matters more than any single "magic" food. Vomiting drains water and salts from your body, alcohol has already irritated your stomach lining, and your stomach may be emptying more slowly than usual. Rushing into a big breakfast is the most common way people end up throwing up a second time. This guide walks through the full rehydrate-first sequence, what to eat at each stage, what to avoid, and the signs that mean it's time to stop managing this at home.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most alcohol-related vomiting settles within several hours. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any liquids down for several hours, the vomiting continues into the next day, you see blood or dark material that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or constant belly pain, or you're very dizzy, confused, or haven't peed in about eight hours. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has been drinking is vomiting while hard to wake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has bluish or pale cold skin, or has a seizure. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't leave them alone, and roll them onto their side so they can't choke. If you drink heavily every day and start vomiting, shaking, and sweating when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor, not a home remedy. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Your Body Needs a Careful Restart After Vomiting

It helps to know what's going on, because it explains why the order of foods matters.

**Alcohol irritates your stomach.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and inflames the stomach lining. Doctors call this inflammation gastritis, and a heavy night can bring on a short-term version of it. An irritated stomach is touchy, which is why rich or acidic food can set it off again.

**Your stomach may empty slowly.** Heavy drinking can slow the rate at which your stomach passes food along to your intestines. Food sits there longer, which adds to the queasy, full feeling and makes a large meal a bad bet.

**Vomiting takes water and salts with it.** Every time you throw up, you lose fluid along with electrolytes, the dissolved minerals like sodium, potassium, and chloride that your muscles and nerves need to work properly. Alcohol also makes you pee more, because it blocks a hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Put those together and you can get dehydrated fast. That's a big part of the headache, dizziness, and weakness. Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains this in more detail.

**Your blood sugar may be low.** Processing alcohol can interfere with the liver's ability to release sugar into your blood, especially if you didn't eat much the night before. Low blood sugar adds to shakiness, sweating, and that hollow, weak feeling. A small amount of simple carbohydrate, once you can keep it down, often helps.

So the job isn't really "eat something to soak up the alcohol." By the time you've thrown up, the main tasks are to replace fluid and salts, let your stomach calm down, and then give it fuel that's easy to digest.

## Step 1: Give Your Stomach a Short Break (First 15 to 30 Minutes)

Right after vomiting, your stomach is at its most irritable. Putting anything into it straight away, even water, can trigger another round.

What to do in this window:

- **Rinse your mouth** with water and spit it out. Stomach acid is harsh on your teeth and throat. Wait about 30 minutes before brushing, since brushing right after acid exposure can wear down softened enamel.
- **Sit upright or lie on your side** rather than flat on your back. Fresh air and a cool cloth on your neck or forehead help some people.
- **Breathe slowly.** Slow, steady breathing can take the edge off nausea.
- **Don't take a painkiller yet.** Anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that's already inflamed. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but has its own issues with alcohol and the liver. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers when it's reasonable.

## Step 2: Sip Fluids, Slowly (The Next Hour or Two)

This is the most important step. Dehydration is the problem most worth fixing, and the method matters as much as the drink.

**Sip, don't gulp.** Take one or two small sips every few minutes, or let ice chips melt in your mouth. A large amount of fluid hitting an irritated stomach all at once is a common trigger for vomiting again. If you keep small sips down for 20 or 30 minutes, gradually increase the amount.

**The best drinks, in rough order:**

| Drink | Why it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte, store brands, or homemade) | Designed to replace water plus sodium and potassium in the right balance | The closest match to what you lose when you vomit |
| Plain water | Easy, always available | Fine on its own, especially if you'll be eating salty crackers or broth soon |
| Clear broth (chicken, vegetable, or bone broth) | Fluid plus sodium, and it feels like food | Warm, not hot. Great bridge between drinking and eating |
| Sports drink, half-diluted with water | Some sodium and sugar | Full-strength versions are sugary and lower in sodium than rehydration drinks |
| Weak ginger or peppermint tea | Soothing, and ginger has some evidence for nausea | Let it cool to warm |
| Ice pops or frozen rehydration pops | Very slow intake, which suits a touchy stomach | A handy trick if sips keep coming back up |

Oral rehydration solutions are what doctors use for dehydration from stomach bugs, and the same logic applies here: your body absorbs water better when it comes with the right amount of salt and sugar. If you don't have any, our [homemade electrolyte drink recipe](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) uses kitchen ingredients. For a comparison of the popular options, see our guide to [electrolyte drinks for hangovers](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared). And if sipping is too much, [Pedialyte popsicles](/never-hungover/pedialyte-popsicles-hangover) are a slower, gentler way in.

**What not to drink yet:**

- **More alcohol.** A "hair of the dog" drink only postpones the hangover and keeps irritating your stomach lining.
- **Coffee and energy drinks.** Caffeine stimulates stomach acid and can upset an inflamed stomach. If you depend on caffeine and feel a withdrawal headache coming, a few sips of weak tea later in the day is gentler than a large coffee.
- **Fizzy drinks.** The bubbles can add bloating and pressure. If flat ginger ale is the only thing that appeals, let it go flat and sip it, but know that most commercial ginger ale contains little real ginger.
- **Orange juice and other acidic juices.** The acid can sting an irritated stomach and throat.
- **Milk, in large amounts.** Some people find dairy heavy on a queasy stomach. A little in tea is usually fine.

**How you know you're rehydrating:** you start to pee again, and the color shifts from dark yellow toward pale straw. Dizziness when you stand up eases. Your mouth feels less dry.

## Step 3: Clear Liquids That Count as Food (Once Sips Stay Down)

When you've kept fluids down for an hour or so and feel a bit better, broth is the ideal next move. It gives you fluid and sodium together, it's warm and comforting, and it doesn't ask much of your stomach.

Good options:

- **Chicken or vegetable broth**, plain or with a pinch of salt
- **Miso soup**, which is light and salty
- **Bone broth**, if you have it
- **A thin soup** like chicken noodle with soft noodles, once plain broth sits well

Our guide to the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) has more ideas, from simple broths to traditional recipes.

## Step 4: Bland Starches (Usually a Few Hours After Vomiting)

Once broth stays down and you feel even a little hungry, it's time for real food. Start small. A few crackers is a better first test than a full plate.

**The best first foods are bland, low in fat, and low in fiber.** They digest quickly, they're easy on an irritated stomach, and they give you carbohydrate to steady your blood sugar.

- **Saltine crackers.** The classic for a reason. Dry, plain, and the salt helps replace what you lost. Our guide to [toast and crackers for a hangover](/never-hungover/toast-and-crackers-for-hangover) explains why they work so well as a first food.
- **Dry toast.** White bread is gentler than whole grain right now. Skip the butter at first, or keep it to a thin scrape.
- **White rice.** Plain or with a little salt or broth.
- **Bananas.** Soft, easy to digest, and a good source of potassium, one of the minerals vomiting and frequent peeing drain. See our [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) guide.
- **Applesauce.** Gentle, slightly sweet, and easy to eat when chewing feels like too much.
- **Plain oatmeal** made with water. Soft and filling, and a good choice once crackers sit well.
- **Plain boiled potatoes**, without butter or sour cream.

### What about the BRAT diet?

You've probably heard of the BRAT diet: bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast. Those four foods are sensible choices for the first few hours, which is why they show up on so many lists. But pediatric and medical groups have moved away from recommending BRAT as a diet in its own right, because eating only those foods for long leaves you short on protein, fat, and nutrients your body needs to recover. Treat BRAT as a starting point, not a plan for the whole day.

## Step 5: Add Gentle Protein (Later in the Day)

Once bland starches are staying down, add some protein. It keeps you full longer, helps you feel less shaky, and makes the next meal easier.

Easy proteins to try:

- **Scrambled or boiled eggs.** Soft, easy to digest, and a good source of protein. Eggs also contain cysteine, an amino acid your body uses to make the antioxidant glutathione, though there is no good evidence that eating eggs speeds up hangover recovery on its own. More in our [eggs for hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) guide.
- **Plain chicken**, baked, poached, or in soup.
- **Plain yogurt**, if dairy agrees with you. Start with a few spoonfuls.
- **Tofu or a mild fish** like baked white fish.
- **Smooth peanut butter on toast**, a small amount once your stomach is clearly settled.

By the evening, most people can eat a normal, moderate meal. Keep it simple and not too large, and stop when you feel full.

## Foods to Avoid for the First Day

Some foods are well known for setting off a sensitive stomach. Skip these until you feel back to normal.

- **Greasy and fried food.** The classic hangover fry-up is a bad idea right after vomiting. Fat slows stomach emptying even more and is a common trigger for nausea. Our guide to [greasy food for a hangover](/never-hungover/greasy-food-hangover) looks at why the craving doesn't match what your body needs.
- **Spicy food.** Chili and hot sauce can irritate an inflamed stomach lining and worsen heartburn.
- **Acidic food.** Tomato sauce, citrus fruit, vinegar-heavy dressings.
- **High-fiber and gassy food.** Raw vegetables, beans, bran cereal, and cabbage can cause bloating and cramping on a sore stomach.
- **Very sweet food.** A pastry or a large soda on an empty, irritated stomach can make nausea worse for some people.
- **Large portions of anything.** Small amounts every hour or two beat one big meal.

## Does Ginger Help?

Ginger is the most popular natural remedy for nausea, and it has real research behind it. Clinical trials have found it helpful for nausea in pregnancy and in some people having chemotherapy or surgery. There's very little research on ginger specifically for alcohol-related nausea, so it's reasonable to try but there is no good evidence that it fixes a hangover.

Easy ways to use it:

- **Ginger tea**, made from fresh sliced ginger steeped in hot water, then cooled to warm
- **Ginger chews or crystallized ginger**, a small piece at a time
- **Real ginger ale or ginger beer**, flat, sipped slowly (check the label, since many brands contain little ginger)

Peppermint tea is another gentle option that some people find soothing. See our full guide to [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) for more.

## A Sample Timeline for the Day After Vomiting

Everyone recovers at a different pace, so treat this as a rough guide, not a schedule to follow to the minute.

| Time after last vomiting | What to have |
|---|---|
| 0 to 30 minutes | Nothing to swallow. Rinse your mouth, rest, sit upright. |
| 30 minutes to 2 hours | Small sips of an oral rehydration drink or water every few minutes. Ice chips or frozen pops if sips don't stay down. |
| 2 to 4 hours | Clear broth. Keep sipping fluids. |
| 4 to 6 hours | A few saltine crackers, dry toast, a banana, or applesauce. |
| 6 hours and later | Rice, oatmeal, scrambled eggs, plain chicken, soup. |
| Evening or next day | A normal, moderate meal if you feel well. Keep avoiding greasy and spicy food until your stomach is back to normal. |

**If you vomit again at any stage, go back a step.** Rest your stomach for 15 to 30 minutes, then restart with small sips. One more episode isn't a reason to panic. Repeated vomiting where nothing stays down for several hours is a reason to get medical help.

## What If You Can't Keep Anything Down?

Sometimes even sips come straight back up. A few things to try at home:

- **Go smaller.** A teaspoon of fluid every five minutes, or ice chips only.
- **Try cold.** Cold drinks and frozen pops are often easier to keep down than room-temperature ones.
- **Change position.** Sit upright, or lie on your left side with your head raised, rather than flat.
- **Avoid strong smells.** Cooking smells, perfume, and cigarette smoke can all set off nausea.

If none of that works and you haven't kept fluids down for several hours, see a doctor or visit urgent care. They can give fluids through an IV and prescription anti-nausea medicine, which works faster than anything you can do at home. Don't wait it out for a whole day, because dehydration builds on itself: the more dehydrated you get, the more nauseated you tend to feel.

### A note on over-the-counter nausea medicine

Some people reach for over-the-counter remedies. Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) contains a salicylate, a relative of aspirin, so it may not be the best choice for a stomach already irritated by alcohol, and it isn't suitable for people who are allergic to aspirin or take blood thinners. Antihistamine motion-sickness pills like dimenhydrinate (Dramamine) can cause drowsiness, which adds to any alcohol still in your system. If you're unsure, ask a pharmacist before taking anything, and read the label.

## When Throwing Up After Drinking Is More Than a Hangover

Most vomiting after a night out is your body reacting to more alcohol than it could comfortably handle. It's unpleasant but passes. Some signs point to something more serious.

**Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking:**

- Is vomiting while confused, very hard to wake, or passing out
- Is breathing slowly (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or with long gaps between breaths
- Has blue-tinged, pale, or cold, clammy skin
- Has a seizure
- Has a very low body temperature

These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which can be fatal. Someone who's very drunk can choke on their own vomit, so never leave them alone and turn them onto their side. Don't give them coffee or a cold shower to "sober them up." Neither works.

**See a doctor soon if:**

- **There's blood in your vomit,** whether bright red streaks or dark material that looks like coffee grounds. Forceful vomiting can tear the lining of the food pipe, and alcohol can also cause stomach bleeding. Read our guide to [vomiting blood after drinking](/never-hungover/vomiting-blood-after-drinking) for what the different appearances mean.
- **You're throwing up green or yellow fluid over and over.** Some bile is common once your stomach is empty, but repeated bile vomiting that won't stop needs attention. Our guide to [throwing up bile after drinking](/never-hungover/throwing-up-bile-after-drinking) explains when it's normal and when it isn't.
- **You have severe belly pain,** especially pain in the upper belly that spreads to your back, which can be a sign of an inflamed pancreas.
- **You show signs of serious dehydration:** no pee for eight hours or more, a racing heart, dizziness or fainting when you stand, or confusion.
- **The vomiting lasts beyond a day.**

**A note for regular drinkers:** if you drink heavily most days and notice vomiting along with shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you cut back or skip drinking, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor instead of trying to manage it with food and fluids alone. Your doctor can help you cut down safely.

## How to Avoid a Repeat Next Time

The most reliable way to avoid throwing up from drinking is the obvious one: drink less, drink more slowly, and stop earlier. A few habits make a real difference:

- **Eat a proper meal before you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Our guide to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the best options, and our page on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why skipping dinner hits so hard.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour. Drinking faster than that is how alcohol builds up past the point your stomach will tolerate.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between drinks slows your pace and keeps you better hydrated.
- **Watch out for mixing and shots.** Drinking games and rounds of shots are the classic way to overshoot without noticing.
- **Have a rehydration drink before bed** if you've had a big night.

For a fuller look at the habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### Where DHM fits, honestly

Some people take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Lab and animal studies suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol, but human research is still limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents vomiting or stops you getting sick from drinking too much. It won't make up for drinking past your limit. If you want to try it as one part of a sensible routine alongside food, water, and pacing, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Don't take any supplement while you're actively vomiting; wait until you can keep food and fluids down.

## The Bottom Line

- **Fluids first, food second.** Rest your stomach for 15 to 30 minutes, then sip an oral rehydration drink or water slowly.
- **Move up in steps:** sips, then clear broth, then bland starches like crackers, toast, rice, bananas, and applesauce, then gentle protein like eggs and chicken.
- **Skip greasy, spicy, and acidic food, coffee, fizzy drinks, and more alcohol** until your stomach settles.
- **If you vomit again, go back a step** and restart with small sips.
- **Get medical help** if you can't keep fluids down for several hours, see blood, have severe belly pain or signs of serious dehydration, or the vomiting lasts beyond a day. Call 911 for signs of alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What should I eat after throwing up from drinking?**

Start with fluids, not food. Wait 15 to 30 minutes after the last time you vomited, then take small sips of water or an oral rehydration drink. Once those stay down for an hour or two, move to clear broth, then plain starches like saltine crackers, dry toast, white rice, a banana, or applesauce. Add gentle protein such as scrambled eggs or plain chicken later in the day once your stomach has settled.

**How long should I wait to eat after throwing up from alcohol?**

Give your stomach about 15 to 30 minutes of rest, then start with small sips of fluid. Most people do best waiting until they've kept liquids down for an hour or two before trying solid food. There's no fixed clock, so let your stomach lead: if you feel hungry and the nausea has eased, try a few crackers. If you vomit again, go back to sips and wait longer.

**What should I drink after throwing up from drinking?**

An oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte is the best match, because it replaces the water, sodium, and potassium you lose when you vomit. Plain water is fine too, and so is a sports drink diluted with some water, clear broth, or weak ginger or peppermint tea. Sip small amounts every few minutes instead of gulping. Avoid more alcohol, coffee, and fizzy drinks until your stomach settles.

**Is it better to eat or not eat after vomiting from alcohol?**

You don't need to force food right away, but you shouldn't go all day without eating either. Fluids come first because dehydration is the biggest problem. Once fluids stay down, a small amount of bland carbohydrate helps steady your blood sugar and usually eases the shaky, weak feeling. Going many hours with nothing can make nausea and headache worse.

**Is the BRAT diet good after throwing up from drinking?**

Bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast are reasonable first foods because they are bland, low in fat, and easy to digest. Doctors no longer recommend living on the BRAT foods alone for long, because they're low in protein and some nutrients. Use them as a starting point for the first few hours, then add eggs, chicken, yogurt, or soup as you feel better.

**What foods should I avoid after vomiting from alcohol?**

Skip greasy, fried, and heavily spiced food for the first day, along with acidic things like orange juice and tomato sauce, and large meals of any kind. Hold off on coffee, energy drinks, and fizzy drinks until your stomach is calm. And don't drink more alcohol, including a 'hair of the dog' drink. It irritates the stomach lining and delays recovery.

**When should I see a doctor after throwing up from drinking?**

Get medical help if you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you see blood or material that looks like coffee grounds in your vomit, you have severe or constant belly pain, you're very dizzy, confused, or not peeing, or the vomiting keeps going into the next day. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is vomiting while hard to wake, breathing slowly, or seizing, because those are signs of alcohol poisoning.
